title: Laws of Motion — Chapter Summary
intro: This chapter is the heart of dynamics. Newton's three laws explain why bodies move the way they do, introduce momentum and impulse as key vector quantities, and set up the conservation principle that powers every collision and rocket calculation in physics. We finish with friction and the standard recipe for solving Newton's-laws problems on inclines and connected systems.

sections.heading: Force and inertia
bullets: Force: a vector push or pull that can change motion.
SI unit: newton (N) = kg·m/s².
Inertia: resistance to a change in state of motion. Mass = quantitative measure of inertia.
Three kinds: inertia of rest, of motion, of direction.
More mass → more inertia → harder to accelerate.

sections.heading: Newton's first law
bullets: A body continues in rest or uniform straight-line motion unless a net force acts.
Defines what a force is: anything that changes the state of motion.
Holds only in inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.
Friction explains why objects on Earth slow down — not the absence of motion-conserving physics.
Also called the law of inertia.

sections.heading: Newton's second law
bullets: Net force = rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt.
For constant mass: F = ma.
1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s².
Linear momentum p = mv; SI unit kg·m/s; vector quantity.
Impulse J = ∫F dt = Δp; airbags / crumple zones use long Δt to reduce peak F.

sections.heading: Newton's third law
bullets: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
Action and reaction act on DIFFERENT bodies and so don't cancel.
Examples: walking (foot ↔ ground), recoil of a gun (gun ↔ bullet), rocket (gas ↔ rocket).
The horse–cart 'paradox' is resolved by separately analysing each body's force balance.
Pairs are of the same kind (both gravity, both contact, etc.).

sections.heading: Conservation of linear momentum
bullets: In an isolated system, total p is constant.
Follows directly from Newton's third law: internal action–reaction pairs cancel.
Holds in any collision, regardless of energy losses.
Recoil: m_g v_g = m_b v_b (gun + bullet from rest).
Inelastic stick collision: m₁ u₁ + m₂ u₂ = (m₁ + m₂) v.

sections.heading: Friction
bullets: Static friction f_s ≤ μ_s N — adjusts itself to balance applied force up to a maximum.
Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N — acts when surfaces are sliding.
μ_k < μ_s for the same surfaces — harder to start than to keep sliding.
Independent of contact area; proportional to N.
Useful (walking, braking) and harmful (energy loss, wear).

sections.heading: Problem-solving recipe
bullets: Identify each body separately.
Draw a free-body diagram for every body.
Choose convenient axes (often along/perp to expected motion).
Write F_net = ma along each axis.
Apply constraints (e.g. inextensible rope means same a; floor blocks penetration so N adjusts).
Solve algebraically.

key_takeaways: 1st law: no net force → no change in motion.
2nd law: F = dp/dt, equivalently F = ma for constant mass.
3rd law: action ↔ reaction on different bodies; they don't cancel.
Linear momentum p = mv is conserved in isolated systems.
Impulse J = Δp; long contact time → small peak force (crumple zones, airbags).
Friction: static max = μ_s N; kinetic = μ_k N; μ_k < μ_s.

glossary.definition: A push or pull (vector) that tends to change the state of motion of a body.
SI unit of force: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
The property by which a body resists changes in its state of motion; mass measures it.
A frame of reference at rest or in uniform motion; Newton's laws hold in such frames without pseudo-forces.
The vector p = mv; SI unit kg·m/s.
The integral J = ∫F dt of a force over time; equals the change in momentum.
A body continues in rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force.
F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass F_net = ma.
Every action is accompanied by an equal-and-opposite reaction on a different body.
In an isolated system (no external net force) the total linear momentum is constant.
A sketch of a single body showing all external forces acting on it as arrows.
Friction force that balances applied force up to a maximum μ_s N when surfaces are not yet sliding.
Friction force μ_k N when surfaces are sliding past each other; independent of speed (approximately).
Ratio μ of friction force to normal force; depends on the pair of surfaces.
The inclination at which a block on a rough plane is just on the verge of slipping; tan θ_r = μ_s.
